newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Wessex yr profits up, targets leaks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Wessex yr profits up, targets leaks.

text.p: Britain's Wessex Water Plc provided a strong finale to the flood of annual water company results on Wednesday with higher profits and dividend and an assurance it was on track to meet "sensible" targets for cutting leaks.

In a statement, Wessex said it was on course to meet a target of cutting leaks to 15 percent of supplies by 2005 from current levels of 23 percent, which should allow it to meet "any sensible mandatory targets."

The company turned in pretax profits for the year ending March 31 of 145 million pounds ($241.9 million), up eight percent and within expectations, and paid out a total dividend of 18 pence per share, which compared with 15.2 pence and was ahead of forecasts.
"They were a pretty good set of figures, momentum in the core business is still going strong," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
Wessex is the last of Britain's privatised water and sewerage companies to report results for the last year, with all of them raising dividends and most improving profits.
Shares in Wessex were up 2.5 pence to 389 pence by 0943 GMT, after touching a high of 395 pence earlier.

Chairman Nicholas Hood said the dividend rise reflected the performance of the non-core business and at the core water business - particularly in cutting costs, as well as a reduction in the number of shares in issue after a buyback earlier this year.
He added that leakage of water was not such an issue for Wessex as for other firms as it had not had supply problems.
"We've got no problems with interruptions to supply...we've never had any for 25 years, we won't have any this year or next year," he said.
Hood added that he saw "no reason why (a mandatory leakage target) should be any lower or higher than the one which we have set for ourselves."
Mandatory targets for cutting leaks are part of a 10-point plan for the industry drawn up by the new Labour government in an attempt to tackle the country's current drought, the worst for 200 years.

The government, which jumped to power with a huge majority on May 1, has also vowed to levy a one-off tax on the "excess profits" of privatised utilities with details expected in its first budget on July 2.
Hood said he wanted the so-called "windfall" tax to favour companies which had performed well.

"Those companies which have performed very well by not having any exceptional provisions for instance for non-core activities, by not having restructuring provisions...should not be penalised, they should be favoured," he said.
As a result, he argued, Wessex should be taxed on an earlier valuation, "closer to privatisation than maybe current valuations."
Analysts said Wessex, which has very low debt compared to equity, might contemplate a further buyback of shares after spending 185 million pounds on one operation this year.
It made the move after its plans to bid for its colleague South West Water were blocked by the previous Conservative government, along with a rival offer from Severn Trent, last year.
"In the absence of any diversification and as long as the windfall tax is not too savage, I would expect a buyback over the next year," the analyst said.
Hood would not be drawn on any possible plans for capital restructuring or acquisitions.
"Obviously within the UK water-to-water combinations of any size is off, but I can't answer what the intention is of the company so far as such a strategic move is (concerned)," he said.
The company said its diversified businesses were doing well with its UK Waste waste management company "positioned for further profit growth."
It said it was in "an excellent position to continue delivering growing shareholder value."
